_about: Words for the engagement PDFs: the one-page overview (downloads/neil-catton-how-an-engagement-runs.pdf, linked from Services) and the guide (downloads/neil-catton-engagement-guide.pdf). Carried over from the September 2026 PDFs. {{years}} and {{sectors}} are filled in by tools/build-pdfs.mjs from site.json. Edit here, then npm run pdfs.
title: How an engagement runs
standfirst: A one-day board briefing and a year-long fractional role run the same arc, at different speeds.
foundation: Every phase draws on the same base: {{years}} years across {{sectors}} sectors, working at both ends of the problem. The outside judgement of non-executive and advisory roles, and the inside delivery of fractional and interim leadership. What changes phase to phase is which lens is doing the work.

phases.name: Read the system
phases.sub: Understanding the organisation as it actually runs
phases.summary: Before any recommendation, the real constraints need to be visible: not the org chart, but how decisions actually get made and what's already been tried. Stakeholder conversations across the business, technology and the board, a review of existing strategy, and a diagnostic that maps dependencies rather than assuming them.
phases.description: Before any recommendation, the real constraints need to be visible: not the org chart, but how decisions actually get made, where authority sits, and what's already been tried. This phase is about listening long enough to see the system clearly, not confirming what's already assumed.
phases.timeframe: Days to weeks, depending on engagement scope
activities: Stakeholder conversations across business, technology and the board
Review of existing strategy, architecture and governance documents
Mapping of decision rights, dependencies and known constraints
Technical and operational due diligence where relevant
Synthesis of findings into a single, shared picture
deliverables: A single view of the system as it actually operates

phases.name: Name what's true
phases.summary: The findings go to the board or founder directly, including the parts that are uncomfortable. No softened language, no burying the real risk in a longer list of minor ones. The evidence is structured into the few things that actually matter, and put in front of the people who need to hear them.
phases.description: The findings go to the board or founder directly, including the parts that are uncomfortable. No softened language, no burying the real risk in a longer list of minor ones. This is the phase most engagements shorten; it's the one that makes everything after it useful.
phases.timeframe: Typically a single session, once the diagnostic is complete
activities: Structuring findings into a clear, evidenced assessment
Naming the two or three things that matter most, not twenty
A direct conversation with the board, founder or sponsor
Agreeing what "true" means before moving to a plan
deliverables: A shared, agreed statement of the real problem

phases.name: Set the direction
phases.sub: A plan that's sequenced and resourced
phases.summary: Direction only means something once it has been tested against what the organisation can actually deliver. The assessment becomes a plan: priorities in order, resourcing made explicit, and a sequence built on real capacity rather than an ideal timeline.
phases.description: Direction only means something once it's been tested against what the organisation can actually deliver. This phase turns the assessment into a plan: priorities in order, resourcing implications made explicit, and a sequence that reflects real capacity rather than an ideal timeline.
activities: Prioritising against impact, risk and delivery capacity
Building a phased roadmap with realistic sequencing
Identifying capability, resourcing and governance gaps
Testing the plan with the people who'll have to deliver it

phases.name: Lead the change
phases.sub: Embedded leadership, not a handover of slides
phases.summary: This is where most technology advice fails: the plan is handed over and the advisor leaves. Here the leadership continues, embedded in the organisation, making the calls, adjusting the plan as reality intervenes, and carrying accountability for the outcome rather than the recommendation.
phases.description: This is where most technology advice fails: the plan is handed over and the advisor leaves. Here, the leadership continues: embedded in the organisation, making the calls, adjusting the plan as reality intervenes, and carrying accountability for the outcome rather than the recommendation.
phases.timeframe: Ongoing: weeks to months, set by the mandate
activities: Fractional or interim leadership of the delivery effort
Day-to-day decision-making within the agreed mandate
Regular reporting to the board or sponsor
Course correction as the programme meets reality

phases.name: Leave it capable
phases.summary: The engagement ends by design, not by attrition. Decisions, rationale and context are documented and handed back deliberately, so the work doesn't quietly need me again next year. This is what separates fractional leadership from consultancy dependency.
phases.description: The engagement ends by design, not by attrition. Capability, decisions and context are handed back to the organisation deliberately, so the work doesn't quietly need me again next year. This is what separates fractional leadership from consultancy dependency.
phases.timeframe: Final one to two weeks of the engagement
activities: Documenting decisions, rationale and open risks
Transferring capability to the team taking over
Formal handover to the board or successor
Agreeing what "done" looks like before leaving
deliverables: A capable team, not a dependency
